chunks: Braking a motor with half/H-bridges. The question: How can you brake a motor using a half-bridge? What about an H-bridge? Which can brake the motor faster?
How does this stress the motor?
A spinning motor is also a generator: it makes its own voltage, called back-EMF, that grows with speed.
To brake it you give that voltage a path to push current through, or you drive the motor backward.
Shorting the two motor wires together is one way; applying reverse voltage ("plugging") is a harder, faster one.
A half-bridge can only short the motor, while an H-bridge can do both.
Picture a heavy flywheel spinning in a workshop. You can let it coast, drag a gentle brake pad on it, or throw the machine into reverse.
The brake pad grips hardest when the wheel is fast and fades as it slows.
Reverse gives a much harder stop, but it strains the gears and the engine, and if you keep the reverse on after the wheel stops, it spins up backward.
The analogy leaves out one thing: with a motor, plugging also draws extra energy from the supply.
With both low-side FETs on, the motor terminals are shorted through the two FETs and the ground path.
The rotating armature (E) pushes current round this loop; the current is E over (R a plus 2R DS(on)) .
After forward drive (current A to B), the braking current flows the other way, B to A through the winding, then down through Q 3 and up through Q 4 , so its torque opposes the rotation.
The high-side devices stay off.
Back-EMF ( E ): the voltage a spinning motor generates, proportional to its speed. Coast: all switches off; only friction slows the motor.
Short-circuit (dynamic) brake: both motor wires tied together; the current is E over R .
Plugging: applying reverse voltage while still spinning; the current is (V plus E) over R . Stall current: V over R , the current when the spinning part (rotor) is held still.
Take a 12 volts motor with 1 ohms winding resistance, spinning at full speed so that its back-EMF is 12 volts. Shorting the wires gives a current of 12 over 1 equals 12 amps.
Plugging adds the supply to the back-EMF, so the current is (12 plus 12) over 1 equals 24 amps, twice as much, and the motor stops faster.
On this page's example motor, plugging stops it in about 35 milliseconds, while the short brake takes about 115 milliseconds to fall to 10% of its speed. That is the whole idea.
"I'd brake with a half-bridge by turning on the low-side FET, which ties both motor terminals to ground, so the back-EMF drives current through the winding and the motor slows.
An H-bridge can do that with both low sides, or can plug by applying reverse voltage, which makes current (V plus E) over R , about twice as much, and stops several times faster.
The stress is peak current, winding heating, a torque jolt on the gears and brushes, and with plugging you must cut the drive at zero speed or it reverses."
Quick check. A half-bridge drives a motor whose other terminal is grounded. Which braking action can it perform?
